strengths: Clearly identifies and quantifies a genuine practical bottleneck (online ViT feature extraction) that has hindered the adoption of joint-encoder rerankers for vision-language retrieval, providing a well-motivated problem statement.

The proposed architecture is simple and modular: any pretrained ViT can be paired with any small language model via a lightweight attention-based token-compression adapter, and only the adapter/LM need be trained, which is data-efficient.

Strong empirical efficiency gains are demonstrated: up to ~53x lower online latency and drastically reduced per-image storage (49kB vs ~1.7-2.4MB for BLIP-family models) while remaining competitive in retrieval accuracy.

Reasonably thorough ablations covering number of compressed tokens, reranking pool size robustness, training-objective components (ITM/MLM/ITC), and local-to-compressed distillation, giving some insight into design choices.
Table 1 shows the reranker consistently improves multiple embedding backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) at varying scales/resolutions, suggesting the approach generalizes as a drop-in reranker.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely a recombination of existing ideas: offline vision-token caching (à la ColBERT/ColPali), VLM-style token concatenation instead of cross-attention (à la LLaVA), and Q-Former-like attention pooling for compression; there is no fundamentally new mechanism.

Evaluation scale is limited despite the "large scale" framing in the title: only Flickr30k (zero-shot) and COCO (fine-tuned) are used, with no experiments on web-scale or million-candidate retrieval that would substantiate large-scale retrieval claims.

Comparisons to prior joint encoders (ALBEF, BLIP, BLIP-2) use models trained on substantially more data (up to 400M pairs) than EDJE (12M), making the "matching prior art" claims not fully apples-to-apples, even though this is disclosed.
No baselines against more recent or alternative efficient reranking/joint-encoder approaches; the comparison set is limited to three older (2021-2023) cross-attention models.
Table 2 (main comparison to prior art) reports only R@1, not the fuller R@1/5/10 breakdown used elsewhere, reducing the completeness of the head-to-head comparison.

No evaluation on other discriminative benchmarks (e.g., VQA, NLVR2) that the compared joint encoders (ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2) are typically evaluated on, leaving open whether EDJE's discriminative power generalizes beyond retrieval.
No code, checkpoints, or reproducibility artifacts are currently available ("will be made publicly available shortly"), limiting verifiability at review time.
No variance/multiple-seed reporting for the retrieval numbers or ablations, making it hard to judge the significance of reported gains (e.g., the distillation and MLM/ITC ablation deltas).

strengths: Clearly identifies and quantifies a real practical bottleneck (expensive online ViT feature extraction) that prevents joint-encoder rerankers like BLIP/BLIP-2 from being used in large-scale retrieval pipelines, and frames the problem well relative to standard practice in text retrieval (cross-encoder reranking).

The overall system design (offline vision-token caching + attention-based token-compression adapter + compact joint encoder) is a reasonable and clearly explained engineering solution, with an architecture figure and taxonomy that aid understanding.
Reports concrete efficiency numbers (storage per image, inference latency, parameter count) alongside accuracy, which is useful for assessing the practicality of the proposed approach.
Ablations on number of compressed tokens, reranking pool size, training objectives, and distillation give some insight into design choices.
weaknesses: The headline comparison to prior joint encoders (Table 2) confounds vision backbone quality with joint-encoder architecture: EDJE uses the much stronger/newer SigLIP2 backbone while ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 use older, weaker ViT backbones trained on less data. It is therefore unclear how much of EDJE's reported accuracy-efficiency advantage comes from the proposed architecture versus simply using a better pretrained vision encoder; a controlled comparison with matched backbones is missing.

The core novelty is incremental: it largely recombines known ideas (caching vision features as in late-interaction retrieval/ColBERT/ColPali, Q-Former-like cross-attention compression, small encoder-only LM replacing a cross-attention fusion block) without a strong new technical insight; the paper itself frames it as mostly an engineering/efficiency repackaging of existing components.

Evaluation is restricted to small, dated benchmarks (Flickr30k, COCO) and pool sizes up to only k=10 (ablated to k=140), far from realistic large-scale retrieval settings (e.g., millions of candidates) that the paper motivates in the introduction; the claimed 50k pairs/sec throughput and web-scale applicability are not actually validated empirically.

Table 1 'improvements' from EDJE over pure embedding-based retrieval are essentially the well-known benefit of reranking within a tiny top-10 pool using the same underlying vision features — this is expected and not a particularly strong or novel empirical finding, yet it is presented as a key result (Q1).

On COCO fine-tuned retrieval, EDJE (even the uncompressed 'local' variant) trails BLIP-2 by a non-trivial margin (e.g., 64.9/81.0 vs 66.3/83.5), so the claim of 'matching prior art' is somewhat overstated, especially after compression further degrades performance.

No code or checkpoints are currently available ('will be made publicly available shortly'), and several implementation details (e.g., how the 50k pairs/sec number is computed, exact verification of reproduced baseline numbers, hard-negative mining potential circularity since the same embedding model is used for both candidate retrieval and training negatives) are not fully specified, limiting reproducibility and raising potential methodological concerns.

No comparison to more recent or alternative multimodal reranking/late-interaction approaches (e.g., ColPali-style models, other recent cross-encoders), nor to generative VLM-based rerankers, leaving the positioning against the current state of the art incomplete.

Results are reported as single numbers without variance across seeds or statistical significance testing, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (especially the smaller ones, e.g., for DFN/MetaCLIP) are meaningful.

strengths: Clearly motivated and practically important problem: existing joint-encoder VLM rerankers (BLIP, BLIP-2, ALBEF) are bottlenecked by expensive online ViT feature extraction, which the paper quantifies convincingly (Figure 1, Section 3.1).

The core idea—precomputing/caching vision tokens offline and using a lightweight attention-based compression adapter plus a compact joint LM for online cross-modal fusion—is simple, well-motivated by analogy to ColBERT/VLM literature, and effectively addresses the identified bottleneck.

Strong efficiency numbers: up to 53x faster inference, drastically reduced per-image storage (49kB vs ~1.7-2.4MB for BLIP/BLIP-2/ALBEF), and far fewer joint-encoder parameters (33M vs 139-167M), while retaining competitive retrieval accuracy on Flickr30k (zero-shot) and COCO (fine-tuned).

Reasonably comprehensive ablations: number of compressed tokens vs. performance trade-off, robustness to reranking pool size, incremental value of each pretraining objective (ITM/MLM/ITC), and benefit of local-to-compressed distillation.

Demonstrated modularity: EDJE improves retrieval when paired with several different embedding backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) at multiple scales/resolutions, suggesting the method generalizes as a drop-in reranker.
Clear writing and useful taxonomy figure situating the work relative to cross-attention models, fully joint models, and modern generative VLMs.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to only two standard, relatively small benchmarks (Flickr30k zero-shot and COCO fine-tuned retrieval); there is no evaluation on larger or more diverse retrieval benchmarks (e.g., web-scale corpora, multilingual retrieval, or harder distractor-rich settings) despite the paper's emphasis on 'large-scale' deployment, and the largest tested reranking pool size is only k=140, far from realistic large-scale scenarios.

Novelty is incremental: the architecture largely recombines existing ideas (offline token caching as in ColBERT/ColPali, VLM-style token concatenation as in LLaVA, and a Q-Former-like cross-attention compression adapter), with the main contribution being the specific combination and efficiency-oriented engineering rather than a fundamentally new technique.

On COCO fine-tuned retrieval, the compressed EDJE variants noticeably underperform BLIP-2 (e.g., 64.6 vs 66.3 T2I R@1, 80.9 vs 83.5 I2T R@1), which somewhat undercuts the claim of 'matching prior art,' particularly since BLIP-2 uses more training data, muddying a fully fair comparison.

Code and checkpoints are not yet released at submission time ('will be made publicly available shortly'), limiting immediate reproducibility and verification of the reported efficiency/storage numbers.
The negative-mining strategy depends on an auxiliary embedding model for hard-negative selection, introducing a dependency whose impact on performance and potential bias is not analyzed.

No comparison against more recent or stronger discriminative/joint baselines beyond ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 (e.g., more modern cross-encoder or hybrid rerankers), and no statistical significance / variance reporting (single-run numbers) across the main results tables.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper cleanly identifies the visual feature-extraction bottleneck in existing joint encoders (BLIP, BLIP-2, ALBEF) as the key obstacle to using them as retrieval re-rankers at scale, backed by concrete timing measurements.

The proposed architecture (offline vision token caching + lightweight cross-attention token-compression adapter + compact MiniLM joint encoder) is simple, modular, and practically motivated, drawing sensible parallels to VLM/LLaVA-style projection and ColBERT-style late interaction.

Extensive empirical validation: results span multiple vision backbones (CLIP, DFN, MetaCLIP, SigLIP2) and scales, zero-shot Flickr and fine-tuned COCO, full-dataset retrieval against LightningDOT, ablations on token count, pool size, training objectives, distillation, cross-model negative mining, quantization, and text-encoder choice.

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: up to 53x faster online inference and drastically reduced storage (49kB/image) relative to BLIP/BLIP-2/ALBEF, with practical considerations addressed (I/O benchmarking, quantization robustness, pseudo-code for deployment).

The interpretability analysis of compressed tokens (nearest-neighbor vocabulary mapping and ColBERT-style alignment scores) provides a nice sanity check that compression preserves meaningful semantic content rather than being a black box.
Good coverage of alternative baselines for token compression (striding, clustering, attention pruning), showing the learned adapter is not a trivial choice.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core techniques (offline vision-token caching, Q-Former-like learned-query cross-attention compression, using a small LM with concatenated vision tokens as in VLMs) are individually well-established in prior literature; the contribution is largely a careful re-combination/engineering effort for the retrieval re-ranking use case rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The main comparison to prior joint encoders (Table 2) conflates architecture efficiency with vision-backbone quality: EDJE is paired with a much stronger, more recent vision backbone (SigLIP2) than BLIP/BLIP-2's ViT-L/16, which likely inflates the apparent competitiveness of EDJE's retrieval accuracy beyond what the architectural changes alone would provide.

Despite the "large-scale" framing in the title, evaluation is confined to small, well-worn benchmarks (Flickr30k, COCO); no evaluation on a genuinely web-scale or noisier dataset (e.g., a LAION/DataComp subset) is provided to substantiate large-scale retrieval claims, and the offline storage/compute cost of encoding billions of images with a strong ViT backbone is not empirically discussed as a limitation.
Gains over some embedding baselines (DFN, MetaCLIP) in Table 1 are quite modest, suggesting the re-ranking benefit is backbone-dependent and not uniformly strong.

The text encoder is fixed to MiniLM for essentially all main experiments, with only a brief, inconclusive appendix ablation (BERT-Base) suggesting minor and mixed effects; deeper analysis of how joint-encoder capacity trades off against efficiency is missing.

Limited discussion of failure modes, qualitative retrieval errors, or scenarios where the compression/token-reduction approach might degrade badly (e.g., fine-grained attribute or counting queries), beyond aggregate recall numbers.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: existing joint/cross-attention VL encoders (BLIP, BLIP-2, ALBEF) are bottlenecked by expensive online ViT feature extraction, which genuinely limits their use as re-rankers at scale.

Simple, clearly described system (offline vision token caching + a learned cross-attention resampler + a tiny MiniLM joint encoder) that yields large wall-clock and storage savings relative to BLIP/BLIP-2/ALBEF.

Extensive set of ablations and auxiliary analyses (number of compressed tokens, re-ranking pool size, training objective components, distillation, quantization of cached tokens, cross-model negative mining, alternative token-reduction baselines, full-dataset retrieval, I/O cost measurements, interpretability of compressed tokens) that go beyond the typical ablation depth of a paper in this space.

The interpretability analysis (nearest-neighbor text tokens for compressed vs. uncompressed visual tokens) is a nice, lightweight diagnostic that supports the claim that compression retains semantically meaningful content.
Reasonably honest limitations section acknowledging the proof-of-concept nature of the work and unexplored directions (multilingual, video, audio).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the design is essentially a combination of two well-known ideas — a Q-Former/Perceiver-style cross-attention resampler (already present in BLIP-2) and the LLaVA-style 'project vision tokens, concatenate with text, let self-attention do the fusion' paradigm — applied with a small MiniLM backbone instead of an LLM. The paper itself acknowledges this lineage but the delta over BLIP-2's Q-Former and LLaVA's projector is incremental.

The central empirical claim of 'matching prior art' is overstated: in Table 2, EDJE (Local) actually underperforms BLIP-2 on COCO fine-tuned retrieval (64.9/81.0 vs. 66.3/83.5) and is comparable to or only marginally better than BLIP on Flickr, despite using a substantially stronger, more modern vision backbone (SigLIP2 vs. BLIP's ViT-L/16). Since backbone quality is a huge confound, the efficiency-accuracy comparison is not well controlled — it is unclear how much of any gain is attributable to the proposed architecture vs. simply swapping in a better pretrained encoder.

The 'precompute vision tokens offline' idea is not new to this paper; LightningDOT, ColBERT/ColPali-style late-interaction caching, and even standard embedding-model indexing already rely on this principle. The paper's main technical addition (the token-compression adapter) is incremental relative to these precedents, and the positioning as solving 'the absence of multimodal re-rankers' overclaims the contribution.

Evaluation is restricted to Flickr30k and COCO, both small, saturated academic benchmarks; despite framing around 'large-scale' web retrieval, there is no evaluation on a genuinely large-scale or more realistic/noisy retrieval corpus (e.g., LAION-scale or a dataset-filtering use case) that would substantiate the large-scale retrieval motivation.

No comparison against other recent efficient or lightweight cross-encoder / re-ranking approaches beyond ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 and a basic LightningDOT baseline; there is no discussion of more modern efficient VLM re-rankers or distillation-based rerankers that might be closer competitors.

Some experimental choices appear to favor the proposed method without fully matched baselines (e.g., different training data sizes between EDJE (14M) and BLIP-2 (400M) are used for the main comparison, and while this is noted, it muddies the fairness of 'matching prior art' claims in either direction).

Minor reproducibility/presentation issues: the code link footnote is left incomplete ('The paper's code is publicly available at'), and several figures/tables (e.g., Fig. 1b, Table 2) mix zero-shot and fine-tuned settings somewhat loosely without fully consistent backbone matching across all baselines, making some comparisons harder to interpret precisely.

strengths: Addresses a clearly motivated and practically important gap: the near-total absence of efficient joint-encoder re-rankers for vision-language retrieval, backed by a convincing bottleneck analysis (vision feature extraction dominates inference cost in BLIP/BLIP-2).

The architectural design is simple, well-justified, and builds logically step-by-step from the identified bottleneck (offline vision token caching + attention-based token compression + lightweight LM with LLaVA-style token concatenation).

Extensive and thorough empirical validation: main results across 4 embedding backbones and multiple scales/resolutions, comparison with ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2 along multiple axes (accuracy, storage, parameters, latency), plus numerous appendix studies (token-count ablation, pool-size robustness, training-objective ablation, cross-model negative mining, full-dataset (LightningDOT-style) retrieval, quantization, alternative text encoders, token-compression baselines, interpretability analysis).

Large practical efficiency gains are well quantified (up to 53x faster inference, order-of-magnitude smaller storage), with concrete system-level considerations (I/O benchmarking for disk-based token retrieval).

The interpretability analysis (nearest-neighbor vocabulary mapping and image-caption alignment scores) is a nice, non-trivial addition that provides evidence the compressed tokens retain meaningful semantic content rather than just compressing blindly.
Good writing and clear structure, with a sensible taxonomy of existing joint-encoder paradigms (Figure 2) that situates the contribution well within related work.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is incremental: the token-compression adapter is conceptually very close to Q-Former/Perceiver-Resampler style cross-attention pooling, and the integration strategy (projecting vision tokens into LM embedding space and concatenating) directly mirrors LLaVA; the core contribution is largely a recombination of known ideas for a new application (re-ranking) rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The main comparison table (Table 2) confounds vision-backbone quality with joint-encoder efficiency: EDJE is paired with a much stronger, more recent frozen backbone (SigLIP2) than ALBEF/BLIP/BLIP-2's own (jointly-trained) ViT-B/L backbones, making it hard to disentangle how much of the accuracy parity is due to the backbone versus the proposed joint-encoder design.

Despite the "large scale" framing in the title, evaluation is restricted to small benchmarks (Flickr30k with 1K images, COCO 5K, and "full" splits of only tens of thousands of images); there is no actual experiment at web-scale (millions+) candidate pools beyond a synthetic I/O-only benchmark in the appendix.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance testing are reported for the main results tables (Tables 1 and 2) or most ablations, despite several reported differences being small (e.g., Table 11 BERT vs MiniLM, or DFN/MetaCLIP gains in Table 1), making it hard to assess robustness of the reported improvements.

Some reported gains are modest or mixed (e.g., COCO fine-tuned I2T for the Local variant is below BLIP and notably below BLIP-2; BERT-Base vs MiniLM ablation shows inconsistent, likely within-noise differences), slightly undercutting the "matching prior art" framing in the abstract.
The code repository link is left empty in the submission ("The paper's code is publicly available at" with no URL), limiting verifiability of reproducibility claims at review time.

The vision encoder is kept entirely frozen and only a lightweight adapter + small LM are trained, which limits the method's ability to improve upon the underlying backbone's representational ceiling; this design choice, while practical, is not deeply analyzed in terms of its fundamental performance ceiling versus fine-tuning.
